subChunks.title: Observer & Strategy Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: The greatest wizards don't hardcode their spells — they carry interchangeable attack strategies and broadcast events to anyone who cares. Observer and Strategy are the patterns that make magic extensible.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Strategy Pattern

Strategy encapsulates an algorithm behind an interface, making it swappable at runtime. The context (here, a Caster) delegates behaviour to a strategy object rather than hardcoding it. This eliminates if/else chains and makes adding new behaviour trivial — just add a new strategy.

interface DamageStrategy {
    int calculate(int base);
}

class NormalHit implements DamageStrategy {
    public int calculate(int base) { return base; }
}

class CriticalHit implements DamageStrategy {
    public int calculate(int base) { return base * 2; }
}

class Caster {
    private final DamageStrategy strategy;
    Caster(DamageStrategy strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
    int attack(int base) { return strategy.calculate(base); }
}

// Usage
Caster normal   = new Caster(new NormalHit());
Caster critical = new Caster(new CriticalHit());
System.out.println("Normal hit: " + normal.attack(50));   // 50
System.out.println("Critical hit: " + critical.attack(50)); // 100

Strategy with Lambdas

Because DamageStrategy is a functional interface, strategies can be expressed as lambdas — no need for separate classes in simple cases.

DamageStrategy poison = base -> base + 15;      // adds poison damage
DamageStrategy empowered = base -> base * 3;    // triple power

Caster poisonCaster = new Caster(poison);
System.out.println(poisonCaster.attack(20)); // 35

The Observer Pattern

Observer (also called Publisher/Subscriber or Event Bus) decouples event producers from consumers. Observers register interest in an event; the subject notifies all registered observers when the event fires — without knowing anything about the observers themselves.

interface SpellObserver {
    void onCast(String spellName);
}

class SpellEventBus {
    private final List<SpellObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>();

    void register(SpellObserver observer) { observers.add(observer); }

    void cast(String spell) {
        observers.forEach(o -> o.onCast(spell));
    }
}

// Concrete observers
SpellObserver logger  = spell -> System.out.println("[Log] Cast: " + spell);
SpellObserver counter = spell -> System.out.println("[Count] Spell fired");

SpellEventBus bus = new SpellEventBus();
bus.register(logger);
bus.register(counter);
bus.cast("Fireball"); // both observers notified

When to Use Each

Strategy: varying algorithm/behaviour at runtime (sort orders, compression strategies, payment methods, attack types). Observer: reacting to events without tight coupling (UI updates, logging, audit trails, event-driven systems). Both rely on programming to interfaces, enabling open/closed principle adherence.

// Strategy: context holds ONE strategy — delegates algorithm
// Observer: subject holds MANY observers — broadcasts events

// Both patterns remove conditionals and enable extension without modification

storyBeats.text: The Academy's battle arena had a problem: every time a new attack type was added, the Caster class needed rewriting. And whenever a spell was cast, a dozen observers — the scoreboard, the combat log, the training monitor — all needed notification.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Strategy is the pattern of the adaptable mage. Instead of hardcoding 'if critical, then double' into the Caster, you hand the Caster a strategy object. Swap the strategy, change the behaviour — the Caster never changes.

storyBeats.speaker: Strategy Pattern
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Observer is the town crier of design patterns. The event bus doesn't care who is listening — it simply announces 'a spell was cast'. The scoreboard, the logger, the counter — each registered observer handles the announcement in its own way.

storyBeats.speaker: Observer Pattern
storyBeats.text:
bus.register(spell -> System.out.println("[Log] " + spell));
bus.cast("Fireball"); // all registered observers notified

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Both patterns honour the Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification. Add a new strategy or observer without touching existing code.
The arena hummed with elegance. New attack types appeared without touching the Caster. New monitors registered without touching the EventBus. The architecture bent without breaking.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Strategy pattern in your own words: what problem does it solve, and how does it eliminate if/else chains? What is the difference between Strategy and Observer — both involve interfaces and multiple implementations, so what makes them distinct in purpose and structure?

Create a Caster class that accepts a strategy. Create both casters with attack(50) and print "Normal hit: 50" and "Critical hit: 100".

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A SOLID principle: classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Strategy and Observer both enable adding new behaviour without changing existing code.
An interface with exactly one abstract method. Strategy interfaces are often functional, allowing lambda expressions instead of explicit class definitions — greatly reducing boilerplate.
A decoupled messaging mechanism where publishers emit events and subscribers react. Libraries like Guava's EventBus, Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher, and Kotlin's Flow implement this pattern.
java.util.Observable and Observer were the original Java observer implementations, deprecated in Java 9 due to design flaws (Observable was a class, not interface). Use custom interfaces instead.
Sometimes called the 'policy' variant of Strategy — emphasises that the strategy defines a rule or policy applied by the context, rather than just an algorithm.
In the Strategy pattern, the 'context' holds a reference to the strategy and delegates work to it. The context's interface stays stable while strategies vary.
Memory leak risk: if observers are registered but never unregistered, the event bus holds strong references preventing garbage collection. Libraries often use WeakReference to avoid this.
Both encapsulate behaviour in an object. Strategy is about varying HOW something is done (algorithm selection). Command is about WHAT is done (request encapsulation, undo/redo, queuing).

questions.questionHtml: What problem does the Strategy pattern primarily solve?
options: It prevents multiple objects from being created from the same class
It eliminates hardcoded algorithm variants by encapsulating them behind a shared interface
It ensures an object notifies its dependants when its state changes
It adds responsibilities to objects without modifying their class
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates hardcoded algorithm variants by encapsulating them behind a shared interface
questions.explanationHtml: Strategy replaces conditional logic (if normalHit... else if critical...) by extracting each algorithm into its own class implementing a common interface. The context selects the algorithm at runtime without knowing its implementation details.

First action() calls Fireball.cast() → "BOOM". Then the strategy is swapped to Heal, so the second action() calls Heal.cast() → "HEAL". Strategy allows runtime behaviour change without modifying Mage.

questions.questionHtml: This Observer implementation has a memory leak risk. What is the issue?
questions.correctAnswer: There is no unregister() method, so observers accumulate in the list and can never be garbage collected
questions.explanationHtml: The observers list holds strong references to every registered observer. Without an unregister() method, observers accumulate indefinitely — especially dangerous when observers are UI components or closures that capture large objects. Add void unregister(SpellObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }.

questions.questionHtml: How does Strategy differ from the Template Method pattern?
options: Strategy uses inheritance; Template Method uses composition
Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in a superclass with steps overridden by subclasses; Strategy swaps entire algorithms via composition at runtime
They are identical — both encapsulate algorithms behind interfaces
Strategy works only with functional interfaces; Template Method works with abstract classes
questions.correctAnswer: Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in a superclass with steps overridden by subclasses; Strategy swaps entire algorithms via composition at runtime
questions.explanationHtml: Template Method uses inheritance: a base class defines the overall algorithm flow, subclasses fill in specific steps. Strategy uses composition: the algorithm is entirely swapped out via an injected interface. Strategy is more flexible (runtime swapping, testable with mocks); Template Method can be simpler for stable algorithmic skeletons.

subChunks.title: Decorator & Command Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: Why create dozens of Spell subclasses for every power combination? Decorator wraps objects in layers like enchanting armour — each layer adding capability without changing the core. Command turns actions into objects you can queue, log, and undo.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Decorator Pattern

Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators implement the same interface as the object they wrap, allowing transparent substitution. You can layer decorators like onion skins — each adding behaviour without subclassing.

interface Spell {
    int power();
    String name();
}

class BasicSpell implements Spell {
    public int power() { return 40; }
    public String name() { return "Basic Spell"; }
}

// Decorator base: wraps another Spell
class SpellDecorator implements Spell {
    protected final Spell wrapped;
    SpellDecorator(Spell wrapped) { this.wrapped = wrapped; }
    public int power() { return wrapped.power(); }
    public String name() { return wrapped.name(); }
}

class EmpoweredSpell extends SpellDecorator {
    EmpoweredSpell(Spell wrapped) { super(wrapped); }
    public int power() { return wrapped.power() + 30; } // adds 30
}

class DoubleCastSpell extends SpellDecorator {
    DoubleCastSpell(Spell wrapped) { super(wrapped); }
    public int power() { return wrapped.power() * 2; }  // doubles
}

// Chaining decorators: (40 + 30) * 2 = 140
Spell spell = new DoubleCastSpell(new EmpoweredSpell(new BasicSpell()));
System.out.println(spell.power()); // 140

Real-World Decorator Examples

Java's I/O streams are the classic decorator example: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(...))) — each layer wraps the previous, adding buffering, charset decoding, and file access.

// Java I/O as Decorator in action:
try (var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in))) {
    // BufferedReader decorates InputStreamReader decorates InputStream
}

The Command Pattern

Command encapsulates a request as an object, separating the sender from the receiver. This enables queuing, logging, undo/redo, and macro recording. Each command knows how to execute and optionally undo its action.

interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

class CastSpellCommand implements Command {
    private final String spellName;
    CastSpellCommand(String spellName) { this.spellName = spellName; }
    public void execute() { System.out.println("Casting: " + spellName); }
    public void undo()    { System.out.println("Undoing: " + spellName); }
}

// Macro command: executes a list of commands in sequence
class MacroCommand implements Command {
    private final List<Command> commands;
    MacroCommand(List<Command> commands) { this.commands = commands; }
    public void execute() { commands.forEach(Command::execute); }
    public void undo() {
        var reversed = new ArrayList<>(commands);
        Collections.reverse(reversed);
        reversed.forEach(Command::undo);
    }
}

Comparing Decorator and Command

Both wrap objects or behaviours — but their purposes differ. Decorator adds responsibilities to an existing object transparently (structural). Command encapsulates a request so it can be stored, queued, and reversed (behavioural). Decorator composites at construction time; Command typically executes at a later, deferred time.

// Decorator: build capability layers at object creation
Spell boosted = new DoubleCastSpell(new EmpoweredSpell(new BasicSpell()));

// Command: create an action, execute it later
Command cmd = new CastSpellCommand("Fireball");
queue.add(cmd);
// ... later ...
cmd.execute();
cmd.undo(); // reversible!

storyBeats.text: The Academy's enchantment workshop faced an explosion of spell combinations: empowered Fireballs, double-cast Frost Novas, triple-empowered Thunderbolts. Writing a subclass for each combination was madness.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Decorator pattern is the art of layering. A BasicSpell exists. An EmpoweredSpell wraps it — adds power. A DoubleCastSpell wraps that — doubles it. Each layer is independent; any combination is possible without a single new subclass.

storyBeats.speaker: Decorator Chain
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Command, on the other hand, turns actions into objects. A spell cast becomes a CastSpellCommand — it can be queued, stored in a macro, executed later, and even reversed.

storyBeats.speaker: Command Pattern
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: You have now seen the grand gallery of patterns. Each one is a template for a recurring design problem — not a rigid rule, but a named solution you can recognise and apply.
The workshop reorganised itself: decorators stacked powers elegantly, commands queued the day's battle spells for execution at dawn. The Academy's architecture had matured from clever to masterful.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Implement the Decorator pattern for spells. Define a Spell interface with int power(). Create BasicSpell (power = 40), EmpoweredSpell (wraps a Spell, adds 30 to its power), and DoubleCastSpell (wraps a Spell, doubles its power).

In main, print three values to show each decorator layer:

  1. System.out.println("Base: " + new BasicSpell().power()); → Base: 40
  2. System.out.println("Empowered: " + new EmpoweredSpell(new BasicSpell()).power()); → Empowered: 70
  3. System.out.println("Double-Empowered: " + new DoubleCastSpell(new EmpoweredSpell(new BasicSpell())).power()); → Double-Empowered: 140
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Decorator pattern: what does it mean to 'wrap' an object, and how is this different from subclassing? Walk through the calculation chain for new DoubleCastSpell(new EmpoweredSpell(new BasicSpell())). Then explain what makes Command different from a simple method call — what additional capabilities does encapsulating a request as an object give you?

From memory, implement the Decorator pattern: a Spell interface with power(), BasicSpell (40), EmpoweredSpell (+30 to wrapped power), DoubleCastSpell (*2 of wrapped power).

Print three lines showing the chain: Base: 40, Empowered: 70, Double-Empowered: 140.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Often confused with Decorator — Composite treats individual objects and groups uniformly (tree structure). Decorator adds responsibilities to a single object. Both implement the component interface but for different reasons.

The canonical real-world example: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(path))). Each class decorates the previous, adding charset handling, buffering, and file access in layers.
Commands stored in a queue can be replayed, audited, or processed by a different thread. Transaction logs in databases are essentially command queues for recovery.
Text editors implement undo via a Command stack: execute() adds to the stack; undo() pops and calls each command's undo() method in reverse order.
A Command that contains a list of other Commands, executing them all as one unit. This is the Composite pattern applied to Command — both structural and behavioural patterns can combine.
The key property of Decorator: since it implements the same interface as the component it wraps, clients cannot tell whether they're using a plain component or a decorated one.
A related behavioural pattern where a chain of handlers each decide to handle or pass a request. Differs from Observer (all observers handle) and Command (one receiver handles a stored request).

A special case of Decorator/Strategy that provides a do-nothing default implementation of an interface. Eliminates null checks: instead of if (observer != null) observer.onCast(), use a NullObserver that does nothing.

questions.questionHtml: What is the key structural requirement for the Decorator pattern to work?
options: The decorator must extend the concrete component class
The decorator must implement the same interface as the component it wraps
The decorator must use static methods
The component must implement Serializable
questions.correctAnswer: The decorator must implement the same interface as the component it wraps
questions.explanationHtml: Decorators implement the same interface (or extend the same abstract class) as the object they wrap. This makes them transparent — clients interact through the interface and cannot tell if they're using a plain object or a decorated one.
b1 applies first: 5 + 10 = 15. b2 applies second: 15 * 3 = 45. This demonstrates manual function composition — the same idea as chaining decorators.

questions.questionHtml: This decorator doesn't pass calls through correctly. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: EmpoweredSpell hardcodes 40 instead of calling wrapped.power() — it should return wrapped.power() + 30
questions.explanationHtml: The decorator hardcodes the base value (40) instead of delegating to wrapped.power(). The correct implementation is return wrapped.power() + 30. With two EmpoweredSpells chained: 40 + 30 + 30 = 100.

questions.questionHtml: When should you use the Decorator pattern instead of inheritance to add behaviour?
options: When the new behaviour is always applied to all objects of the class
When you need to add behaviour dynamically at runtime, or combine multiple optional behaviours in any combination
When you need to override a private method
When you need to share state across all instances
questions.correctAnswer: When you need to add behaviour dynamically at runtime, or combine multiple optional behaviours in any combination
questions.explanationHtml: Inheritance creates a fixed class hierarchy — you'd need a subclass for every combination (EmpoweredDoubleCast, EmpoweredTripleCast, etc.), causing a combinatorial explosion. Decorator allows any combination of behaviours at runtime through composition — the preferred approach in modern Java design.

questions.questionHtml: What capabilities does the Command pattern provide that a direct method call cannot?
options: Queuing, logging, and undo/redo — because the request is encapsulated as an object that can be stored and reversed
Adding responsibilities to an object at runtime without subclassing
Notifying multiple observers when an object's state changes
Swapping algorithm implementations dynamically via a shared interface
questions.correctAnswer: Queuing, logging, and undo/redo — because the request is encapsulated as an object that can be stored and reversed
questions.explanationHtml: A direct method call executes immediately and is gone. Command wraps the request in an object with execute() and (optionally) undo() methods, so it can be stored in a queue, added to a macro, logged to an audit trail, or reversed — none of which are possible with a plain method call.

execute() prints Casting: Fireball. undo() prints Undoing: Fireball. This demonstrates the two core capabilities of Command: executing a stored request and reversing it. The same cmd object could have been queued or passed to a macro before either method was called.
